channel.title: Tangle - the good parts
channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The Russia diesel deal.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Plus, a look back at Justice Clarence Thomas’s confirmation.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Russia diesel deal. On Friday, President Donald Trump announced an agreement to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports in return for Russia releasing roughly 800,000 tons of diesel by the end of November and millions more by an unspecified date. The president said the deal will bring down diesel prices impacted by supply disruptions linked to the Iran war but did not say it is tied to a larger ceasefire deal. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and some U.S. lawmakers criticized the agreement as a gift to Russia and urged Trump to reverse course. 

Back up: In response to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the U.S. and other Western countries leveled broad sanctions on the Russian economy and individual leaders. In September, Congress passed a new set of sanctions — some of which applied to Russia’s energy sector — with strong bipartisan support, and President Trump signed the bill into law. 

Under the announced terms, the U.S. will temporarily remove sanctions on Russian diesel exports, and Russia will immediately supply the U.S. and global marketplace with approximately 300,000 metric tons of the fuel. They’ll supply another 500,000 tons in November and an additional one million tons “immediately thereafter,” according to Trump. The president also said Russia will supply three million additional tons “within a short period of time” based on Russian refinery capabilities. 

President Zelensky immediately spoke out against the deal, saying, “It looks like a happy birthday present for Putin… It shows weakness of the world.” Zelensky also suggested that a U.S. negotiating team had misled Ukrainian officials about Trump’s discussions with Russian President Vladimir Putin over the energy agreement. Other Western leaders also questioned the deal; Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said, “It provides Moscow with legitimacy as its bombs continue ​to fall on Ukrainian cities, generates new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakens the effectiveness of sanctions.”

Separately, on Sunday, President Trump announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia, saying, “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” However, Zelensky indicated that he was not aware of an agreement or the terms of the purported ceasefire, later accusing Russia of attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. 

On Tuesday, a group of six Democratic and six Republican senators sent a letter to Trump asking him to back out of the diesel deal. “[The agreement] will have a negligible impact on fuel prices but the revenues the Kremlin will receive from this agreement will undoubtedly finance its desired war of attrition and advance security cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea,” they wrote. 

Today, we’ll share perspectives from the left and right on the deal, followed by Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left opposes the deal, with some saying it won’t bring down energy prices.
  • Many expect Russia’s war effort will benefit. 
  • Others suggest Trump is selling out Ukraine.

The Guardian editorial board wrote about the “imperative to keep pump prices down.”

“Mr. Trump is unhappy with Ukraine targeting Russian oil refineries. He claims that this is the cause of high energy prices afflicting American consumers and threatening Republican prospects in next month’s midterm elections,” the board said. “The real driver of global energy prices is not Ukraine defending itself from Russian attack, but Mr. Trump’s failing war against Iran. However, the US president is incapable of admitting any fault. 

“Blaming Mr. Zelenskyy enables him to deny his own culpability and, with malevolent encouragement from Mr Putin, to revive the preposterous notion that Ukrainian intransigence rather than Russian aggression is the reason why his promise to broker a peace deal remains unfulfilled,” the board wrote. “The best response to Mr. Trump’s perfidy is for Mr. Zelenskyy’s friends to reaffirm their support… thereby signalling that Ukraine will not be beaten by deals between the Kremlin and the White House.”

In The Philadelphia Inquirer, Trudy Rubin suggested the deal will “fund Putin’s war machine.”

“The ‘diesel deal’ Trump has gifted Putin won’t halt Russia’s aggression. It will reward it,” Rubin wrote. “It will encourage the Kremlin’s unyielding demand that Kyiv surrender to Moscow’s overlordship. And it will fuel Putin’s war chest… The Ukrainians were ready to discuss a two-way ceasefire over attacks on energy infrastructure, but were totally blindsided. Instead, Trump unilaterally declared such a ceasefire had been reached. It hadn’t.”

“Yet when Zelensky rejected the one-sided diesel deal, Trump went ballistic and called for his replacement, as if Ukraine were a banana republic whose president could be ousted overnight,” Rubin said. “If Putin keeps getting freebies from his friend Donald, why make concessions? Lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as Zelensky noted, not only gives Putin ‘more money to inflict suffering on us’ but ‘gives him the ability to fight even more.’”

In The Atlantic, Anne Applebaum said “Donald Trump has dropped all pretense.”

“[President Trump] lifted sanctions on the import of Russian diesel fuel, in violation of the letter and spirit of laws that he himself signed,” Applebaum wrote. “The president has implied that the point of his new policy is to lower fuel prices for Americans. But this is not a sufficient explanation or justification for these dramatic actions. The amount of fuel that Russia could export is too small, the impact on pricing too slight, the narrative too late to shape electoral outcomes. 

“This looks, instead, like something very different: an abrupt, Hail Mary attempt to force Ukraine to surrender and to save the Russian economy, perhaps in order to finally complete the multiple business deals that the Russians are known to have discussed with American negotiators and others in Trump’s orbit,” Applebaum said. “American allies in Europe and elsewhere have tried to explain to the president the significance of the war and the threat that Russia poses... Now it looks as if they have failed, and Trump has followed his oldest instincts to side with Putin.”

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with some calling the deal a strong strategic move. 
  • Others argue that the agreement is a short-term solution to a long-term problem.
  • Still others contend Trump’s deal supports Putin’s war efforts.

In Fox News, Gordon Sondland suggested Trump is “threading the needle.”

“Europe is not yet strong enough to contain Russia without substantial American support. Despite years of promises, too many NATO allies remain dependent on American military capabilities, intelligence, logistics and leadership,” Sondland wrote. “Every additional weapons system, dollar and hour of strategic attention consumed by Moscow is a resource unavailable for deterring Beijing or addressing other threats… Trump is trying to change that equation. 

“In the long run, we want a fully economically engaged Russia that has something meaningful to lose,” Sondland said. “That doesn’t mean trusting Putin. It means understanding his incentives. Putin wants two things: money and real estate. He wants the economic benefits of international engagement and the territorial advantages of an empire. Trump is uniquely positioned to offer the former while making the latter prohibitively expensive. That is the needle Trump is trying to thread.”

In the Daily Caller, David Blackmon wrote about energy’s “long-term problem.”

“Any visible relief at the pump before the mid-terms would matter politically as well as economically,” Blackmon wrote. “But, with just three weeks until Election Day… the same constraints remain: Utilization rates that are not sustainable, thin inventories, and the absence of new domestic refining capacity. Temporary imports and sanctions waivers can buy time, but they do not substitute for permitting and building additional domestic capacity. 

“If the new diesel flows and the energy truce are kept, U.S. consumers will no doubt see some price relief. If any of the deal’s fundamentals fail, the pressure on U.S. refineries continues unabated,” Blackmon said. “Either outcome leaves the central problem intact: The U.S. and the world need more refining capacity than current policies and geopolitics have allowed, and two ongoing wars have robbed markets of all their cushions. Something has got to give.”

The Wall Street Journal editorial board said the deal will “directly finance Mr. Putin’s bloody war.”

“The Financial Times reported Saturday that the Trump Administration ‘threatened to cut off vital intelligence sharing’ to Kyiv if it continues attacking Russian refineries,” the board wrote. “On Wednesday 22 people, including five children, were killed in a Russian cruise missile strike on an apartment building… After the diesel announcement, Russia launched glide bombs Saturday at a residential area of Zaporizhzhia, killing at least 20.”

“Without a complete cease-fire, Russia will continue to torment Ukrainian civilians. The strategic turn here is hard to understand,” the board said. “[Trump’s] multiple attempts at appeasing Mr. Putin… haven’t moved the Russian. On the weekend a Russian official said the diesel deal doesn’t change Mr. Putin’s determination to achieve his war aim, which is to turn Ukraine into a Kremlin satrapy. Until that changes, Mr. Trump’s diesel deal helps Russia and not the cause of peace.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • From President Trump’s standpoint, a deal with Russia could offer a chance to alleviate fuel prices ahead of the midterms.
  • From Putin’s standpoint, Trump is offering major economic relief during a war of attrition with Ukraine.
  • This deal reeks of desperation; it hurts our allies, helps our enemies, won’t lower gas prices, and is probably illegal.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Imagine you are in President Trump’s position. 

At the urging of a Middle East ally, you’ve led the nation into a conflict with Iran that has proved much more difficult to end than you imagined. Iranian forces have been able to disrupt (or, at times, completely shut down) the Strait of Hormuz, a critical chokepoint for oil shipping, something you may have known was possible but never imagined would be so difficult to resolve. Bravado and bombs have not freed up the waterway, nor have quieter tactical negotiations or special operations. As the midterms have inched closer, fuel prices have continued to rise, driving persistent inflation. Despite leading a country that dominates diesel exports, diesel prices have also skyrocketed to the detriment of Americans.

At the same time, you haven’t been able to negotiate a truce between Ukraine and Russia, which you promised you’d do in the first 24 hours of your presidency. Vladimir Putin is an influential, authoritarian leader you harbor a kind of twisted respect for, while Volodymyr Zelensky is a petulant, persistent leader of a less significant country who desperately needs your support but has less to offer in return. You thought Putin would defeat Zelensky, then briefly thought Zelensky would defeat Putin, and now fear that the effective Ukrainian strategy of targeting Russian oil refineries will further disrupt an already fragile global energy supply. And, still, the midterms inch closer.

So you have a predicament. Expensive foreign diesel is not necessarily bad for U.S. producers. In theory, they should benefit from the short supply by making more money refining crude oil into diesel. However, American consumers pay the downstream costs of more expensive diesel: From freight companies paying higher transportation costs to your average Great Plains rancher getting crushed at the pump, the bad outweighs the good. These pains are felt globally, and a lot of world leaders blame you, since you launched a war with Iran, which also disrupted global energy supply. You could definitely use a scapegoat.

The obvious solution to lower prices is to create more supply, and the simplest route is to free up the Strait of Hormuz, allowing more diesel to flow in every direction and bringing down the costs globally. But you have not been able to get the strait back to “normal,” and after several attempts you start to look at the rest of your board: You’ve played your hand in Venezuela, you’ve made major releases from the strategic U.S. oil reserve — that leaves Russia.

Now imagine being in Vladimir Putin’s position: You invaded Ukraine in 2022, plunging Eastern Europe into disarray and sending an economic and energy shock across the globe. When the war started, you were exporting about 40 million tons of diesel per year. The United Kingdom and Europe tried to punish you by not buying your diesel, so you replaced their markets with countries like Turkey, Brazil, and nations across Africa. This worked for a while, and as of April this year, you still had some 3 million tons of diesel per month available to export, or 36 million tons per year.

And then Ukraine opened up a new front in the war. They started bombing your oil refineries, and by September, your export rate was decimated — down to 325,000 tons per month. To avoid a domestic shortage, you banned diesel exports everywhere except Central Asia and Mongolia. You’re weathering the storm, refusing a ceasefire with Ukraine and escalating the war there, hoping that your country can pace its own use of oil to stave off economic calamity until well after Ukraine’s financial ruin.

In walks President Trump. He’s got an offer: Export a few million tons of diesel between now and April 2027, and over that period he will suspend the economic sanctions he has in place to punish anyone buying diesel from you — no strings attached to a ceasefire or peace deal with Ukraine. The diesel you’ll export in the arrangement is worth about $7 billion, and with the sanctions gone, you won’t have to sell it at a discount. For the U.S., this will create more supply in the global system, theoretically bringing down global oil and diesel prices.

There’s your deal.

As for the millions of us American voters and consumers, I have a few frameworks for thinking about this deal: First, is it good for America? According to Reuters, Russia is going to immediately supply 300,000 metric tons (or 2.25 million barrels) of diesel to the United States and global markets. That sounds like an astronomical amount, and I suppose it is. But it’s less than a day’s supply for the U.S. transport sector alone, and it’s going to be dispersed globally. Trump has said Russia will release another 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million after that, which altogether amounts to about four days of the total diesel demand for U.S. transport. 

The Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center suggested the deal might bring prices down marginally, but many market players have already factored in assumptions that Russia would export all the surplus diesel it could — it has no place to store it otherwise. Real price relief would only come if Kyiv stopped bombing Russian refineries, which it isn’t going to do, since it has learned that’s a powerful lever to pull.

And that’s just the benefits. The costs — benefiting a geopolitical rival, undermining a geopolitical ally, and embroiling the U.S. government in yet another questionable international deal — are also real.

That brings me to my second framework: Is President Trump’s deal even legal? The sanctions statute was enacted in 2022 under President Biden. While presidents typically have broad authority to waive sanctions, this specific law was unusual, putting in plain text that the president must first consult with several congressional committees, submit a report 45 days before making changes, and provide certification to Congress before lifting the prohibition. In fact, the entire sanctions relief — by law — is dependent on Russia withdrawing from Ukraine and ceasing hostilities, a determination that must be accepted by Ukraine. None of that has happened, so many legal experts and a bipartisan coalition of Congress say the president broke the law, and they have called for the president to rescind the deal.

Third, and finally, is the larger geopolitical context: Will this meaningfully address the global energy crisis? Remember, Russia’s war didn’t spark the 2026 global energy crisis — Trump’s decision to attack Iran did. The deal itself won’t be much of an economic boon for Russia (the $7 billion of diesel was going to be sold anyway, and at just slightly cheaper rates), but the signal it sends is helpful for Putin. It comes at a time when Ukraine is accusing the U.S. of hampering its battlefield tech and halting shared intelligence about Russian attacks. In sum, we appear to be turning on Ukraine, handing a small but meaningful economic gift to Putin, and doing it all for an uncertain and marginal improvement in energy prices — prices that were destabilized by a different war that we started. 

Oh, and this is all happening a month after the president signed a bipartisan bill that explicitly leveled sanctions and tariffs on countries that buy Russian oil and gas. Trump explained the sudden pivot by saying his number one priority was ranchers, farmers and truckers, and he blamed Ukraine for ignoring requests to stop bombing Russian refineries.

It’s a mess — a genuine election-time Hail Mary that could have long-term negative implications for our international relations (after all, we’ve been punishing countries for buying Russian oil until now) and for the future of Ukraine (which is suddenly dealt yet another disadvantage in the war). I’m open to arguments that this is somehow “good” for us, or the global geopolitical situation, but I’ve seen very little in the way of compelling points to that end. 

Take the survey: Do you think the deal will affect energy prices? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The Ilhan Omar investigation.
item.dc:creator: Will Kaback
item.description: Plus, how Obama’s spat with Fox News compares to Trump’s recent media ban.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Ilhan Omar investigation. On Monday, federal agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) searched Rep. Ilhan Omar’s (D-MN) Washington, D.C. residence as part of an immigration investigation. The Justice Department and Department of Homeland Security have shared minimal information about the cause and outcome of the search, but the probe is reportedly related to paperwork Omar’s father filled out when applying for legal status for their family in the United States. The congresswoman denied any wrongdoing and accused the Trump administration of targeting her for political reasons.

Back up: Omar was born in Somalia and fled the country as a child after the outbreak of civil war in the 1990s. She spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States at age 12 in 1995, and she eventually settled in Minneapolis, Minnesota, becoming a U.S. citizen in 2000. Omar served in the Minnesota House of Representatives before winning election to the U.S. House in 2018. She is the first Somali-American elected to Congress. 

President Donald Trump and Rep. Omar have an adversarial relationship; Trump has questioned her loyalty to America, while Omar has been an outspoken critic of the Trump administration and accused him of racism. The president has also linked Omar to his broader criticisms of Minnesota’s Somali-American community, which he claims is responsible for widespread fraud and other criminal activity. 

On Monday, Trump claimed that he is not involved in the investigation into Omar but called her “totally crooked.” Several outlets have reported that federal agents are looking into whether her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, deliberately misstated her birth year to make her eligible for citizenship at the time he was naturalized. Federal agents are also reportedly investigating whether Mohamed lied on his own immigration paperwork. 

Following the HSI search, Rep. Omar’s office said in a statement, “This raid by Trump’s DHS is an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies. For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back.” House Democratic leadership also condemned the search, saying it is “deeply disturbing and raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.”

Below are views from the right and left on the investigation into Omar. Then, Senior Editor Will Kaback’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with many supporting the probe into Omar’s past.
  • Some suggest the investigation’s stakes are high for Trump and Omar.
  • Others question the Trump administration’s motives.

In the New York Post, Rich Lowry suggested there are “plenty of reasons to probe [Omar’s] past.”

“Much of Ilhan Omar’s family story is a black box, but we are presumably about to learn much more about it,” Lowry wrote. “She has always responded with angry, uninformative dismissals, even when the Minneapolis Star-Tribune — not exactly a right-wing news source — has made inquiries… She gives the impression of wanting to provide as a little information about her family background as possible, and sticking to the more important work of maligning her adopted country.”

“If she’s being smeared, Omar should sit down with a neutral journalist and walk through the details of all this with as many documents as she can muster,” Lowry said. “That seems unlikely. But it’s a certainty that she’ll continue to excoriate the United States — whether it’s the country that welcomed her as a penniless refugee, or the one that tries to denaturalize her for alleged immigration fraud.”

In the Boston Herald, Joe Battenfeld asked “will Trump now turn up the heat on Omar?”

“An embattled President Trump is undertaking a risky gambit raiding the home of controversial ‘Squad’ member Rep. Ilhan Omar just seven weeks before the election,” Battenfeld wrote. “The liberal media is already raising questions about Trump and the DOJ’s political motivations in launching the early morning raid on Omar’s DC residence on Monday. But if the feds do file charges and find Omar is in the country illegally or filed false immigration paperwork it would be a big blow to Democrats and the progressive movement.”

“There is a possibility Omar could be in serious legal jeopardy. An arrogant Omar until now has failed to address her immigration and tax status. She exudes [a] ‘How dare you’ vibe,” Battenfeld said. “Will there be strategic leaks in the investigation? Will Omar’s brother talk? Or will Omar come up with conclusive evidence that she has done nothing wrong?”

In National Review, Andrew C. McCarthy said “I find myself rooting against both sides.”

“I find Omar a detestable figure and have long suspected she may have been complicit in immigration fraud,” McCarthy wrote. “On the other hand, the Trump Justice Department lawfare is revolting: Regardless of whether she’s guilty, Omar is under investigation solely because she is a Trump political enemy. That’s obvious — and not just because of the Trump DOJ’s extensive track record of hounding the president’s nemeses. 

“The DOJ is pursuing an immigration fraud case, and a criminal prosecution arising out of any fraud in Omar’s admission to the United States and subsequent naturalization as a citizen would be long time-barred under the applicable statutes of limitations,” McCarthy said. “Ordinarily, the DOJ would not bother investigating crimes too stale to prosecute, but because Omar is a Trump foe, that protocol has gone by the boards.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left opposes the investigation, with many saying Trump continues to weaponize the Justice Department.
  • Some call the probe an abuse of power.
  • Others argue that the accusations are racially motivated.

In Esquire, Charles P. Pierce said there are “many things wrong with what the DOJ is doing.”

“Representative Omar came to this country as a refugee from Somalia when she was 12. Whatever her father may have done — and I’m going to need a truckload of evidence that he did anything at all — I don’t know what it has to do with her,” Pierce wrote. “Except that she has been the target of abject racial xenophobia ever since she came to Washington.” 

“This is another example of the president weaponizing law enforcement to play out the demonology in his increasingly superfluous brainpan,” Pierce said. “It also is a shocking violation of separation of powers… But many of the Republicans in Congress are just as rabid about Representative Omar as the president is. Their bigotry cannot replace the constitutional order, even under this president.”

In Common Dreams, Robert Reich called the investigation an “abuse of power.”

“In a democracy, the highest officials of one party do not ‘build cases’ to pursue legislators from the opposing party. Nor do they investigate their political opponents within days of an election, in violation of explicit Department of Justice rules,” Reich wrote. “The Department of Justice guidance for protecting election integrity explicitly states that the department should not engage in investigative measures that might ‘chill legitimate voting and campaign activities’ or ‘interject an investigation itself into ongoing campaigns.’”

“The Justice Manual further states that federal prosecutors and agents ‘may never select the timing’ of investigative steps, charges, or public statements for the purpose of affecting an election or giving an advantage or disadvantage to a candidate or political party,” Reich said. “If Democrats regain control of the House, they must investigate this flagrant abuse of power by Trump, Vance, and the Department of Justice.”

In MS NOW, Zeeshan Aleem suggested Omar is “the latest scapegoat.”

“The reality, it should be easy to deduce, is that Trump sees Omar as a convenient target for his white nationalist agenda… He describes Somali immigrants as ‘garbage’ and ‘low-IQ people’ who ought to be kicked out,” Aleem wrote. “While it’s not clear what the potential outcomes of the investigation are, it fits into the Trump administration’s stated agenda to denaturalize citizens more aggressively than any other in history. 

“It’s yet another way for Trump to peddle the fiction that immigrants are the source of our national problems,” Aleem said. “Omar is also a prominent target because she’s a vociferous progressive who is aligned with democratic socialists in Congress on issues such as supporting Medicare for All and cutting off aid to Israel… Trump and his allies, like many reactionaries before them, appear particularly keen on commingling their targeting of people of color with their attacks on left-wing politics.”

My take.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
 
  • I grew up in the district Omar represents, so I’m familiar with her and the state’s Somali immigrant population.
  • President Trump is clearly overstating the issues with that community as part of a broader anti-immigrant agenda.
  • Omar has her own issues, but they don’t justify a politicized investigation, let alone deportation.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Monday’s raid of Rep. Ilhan Omar’s residence is the latest example of the Trump administration’s investigations into political opponents. And just like the targets of those other probes — like James Comey, Letitia James, and Sen. Adam Schiff (D-CA) — Omar’s feud with President Trump is grounded in both ideological and personal grievances.

I grew up in the suburbs of Minneapolis, in the district Omar represents, MN-05. She was never my representative (I was in college when she won the seat in 2018), but I have a good understanding of the district’s political makeup from working on local campaigns in high school and from family and friends who remain her constituents. 

Somali-Americans have an outsized influence in MN-05 and state politics writ large. Growing up, first- or second-generation immigrants from Somalia were my classmates, friends, and teammates. I never really perceived them as a distinct group; they were just classmates, friends, and teammates. If differences existed between us at home, they were rarely present at school or on the field. 

But even though it didn’t register with me as a kid, Minnesota’s Somali community is unique — it’s the largest Somali population in the United States, and MN-05 has the largest Somali population within the state. Many, including Rep. Omar and her family, resettled in the Twin Cities after fleeing the Somali Civil War of the 1990s. The community is still a relatively small part of the overall population (even in MN-05, Somalis make up just 3.4% of residents), but they’ve amassed considerable political influence — similar to other immigrant communities throughout U.S. history (and Minnesota history).

And like those other historical immigrant communities, Somali immigrants’ integration hasn’t been seamless — tensions were brewing long before YouTuber Nick Shirley showed up to document claims of fraud. Now, those tensions are ratcheting up: Just this month, alleged members of a Somali gang were charged in connection with a shooting at a homecoming football game, and the FBI arrested a U.S. citizen of Somali descent for allegedly plotting a mass shooting at the Mall of America. After a separate incident linked to Somali gangs in which over 100 rounds were fired in a suburban area, Bloomington Police Chief Booker Hodges said, “I'm not going to sugarcoat it. We're dealing with Somali-American gangs right now.” Meanwhile, many Somali-Americans in Minnesota report feeling increasingly ostracized and scapegoated for the actions of a few.

Somali-American leaders have spoken openly about how issues like fraud can seem endemic to their group. But Somalis themselves are most often the targets of these bad actors in the community. In 2024, Kayseh Magan, a former Medicaid fraud investigator and Somali-American, explained, “The conduit for fraud in publicly funded programs are the recipients, who require services. Somali recipients face language and cultural barriers. In an unfamiliar country, they lean heavily on other Somalis. Somali providers are in a position of trust, and some have taken advantage.”

As the face of the Somali-American community in Minnesota (and, really, the United States), Ilhan Omar has become an avatar for these problems. For the Trump administration, targeting Omar clearly communicates its broader agenda: push people like her out of the United States.

It’s hard to say if the investigation has merit based on the limited information currently available. We know that agents from Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) had a search warrant to carry out Monday’s raid and that their investigation is probing whether Omar’s father falsified her paperwork when applying for legal status. We also know that the Trump administration has been promising to go after the congresswoman for immigration-related offenses — DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin told conservative podcaster Benny Johnson last month that “something’s going to happen” in relation to Omar, adding, “If we can prove it, that you shouldn't have been here in the first place, we'll deport you.” 

Whatever comes of this investigation, the administration faces an uphill battle on any immigration-related criminal charges. As National Review’s Andrew McCarthy noted under “What the right is saying,” even if investigators found evidence that Omar’s father made misrepresentations in his immigration applications, the statute of limitations for prosecuting immigration crimes expired years ago. Not to mention, any theoretical charges would implicate her father, not Omar herself. In sum, the congresswoman almost certainly can’t be criminally charged for immigration offenses, though a civil denaturalization case is possible but unlikely based on what we know now. And the likelihood that she is denaturalized is slimmer still.

With that said, Omar’s backstory is convoluted. After fleeing Somalia, she spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the U.S. at age 12. In 2018, she told The Intercept that she became a U.S. citizen alongside her father through a process called derivative citizenship. However, just this week, The New York Post reported that Omar’s staff had her birth year changed from 1981 to 1982 after she was elected to Congress. That’s a critical change, because derivative citizenship is only available to minors; and if Omar was born in 1981, she would have already been an adult when her father was naturalized. 

Questions about Omar’s immigration history extend to other rumors about her family. President Trump and conservative activists have alleged that Omar improperly obtained legal status for her brother in the U.S. by marrying him. As documented by Snopes, the rumor originated from a post on an online Somali community discussion forum and has never been substantiated. Still, the saga is complex — Omar says she married a different man (Ahmed Hirsi) in 2002 but did not complete the application process for a civil marriage. She and Hirsi separated in 2008, and she formally married Ahmed Nur Said Elmi (the man said to be her brother) the next year. Omar and Elmi separated in 2011, but did not legally divorce until 2017. Between those two dates, she reconciled with Hirsi. That marriage also failed, and she is now married to political consultant Tim Mynett. It’s a fairly fraught relationship history (fraught enough to help these rumors persist), but still: No evidence has emerged that Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is Omar’s brother. 

Other rumors like this one have also largely been disproven, but I can accept that a narrow immigration investigation into Omar’s citizenship paperwork might have merit (remember, a court had to sign off on HSI’s search). Even accepting that, the Justice Department’s and DHS’s decision to pursue this raid, in spite of the statute of limitations and the proximity to the midterms, screams ill intent — particularly given the DOJ’s traditional (though not explicit or binding) practice of avoiding public actions involving political candidates within 60 days of an election. I don’t think the Trump administration is trying to derail Omar’s chances of reelection — MN-05 is deep blue, and she’s going to win. Rather, this investigation is about sending a message: We’re fighting to push people like Omar out of the U.S. 

It’s a playbook we’ve seen Trump run many times, including his 2024 remarks about Haitian migrants in Ohio eating cats and dogs. These days, he’s saying that Somali immigrants are responsible for “Violence, Murder, and Mayhem all over [Minnesota]” and calling on “the people of Minnesota [to] fight back.” 

Now, in targeting Omar (someone he’s openly fantasized about sending back to Somalia), Trump is acting on personal grievance but also a collective grievance shared by many in the MAGA movement: People like Omar are taking over this country; we need to push them back. It’s a politically salient message, and its power comes from real frustrations. But I draw the line at casting an entire group of people (most of whom are naturalized or native-born U.S. citizens!) as violent criminals who should be forcibly removed.

I’ve held off on sharing my own views on Omar, but now I’ll show my cards: I’m not a fan. She’s made a slew of objectionable remarks in the past — mostly criticisms of Israel that veered into antisemitism — but I’m more opposed to her political style that emphasizes hollow clapbacks tailored for social media clips, personal digs, and attempted gotchas (even when she’s the one in the wrong). This style isn’t unique to Omar; I’m against it in all cases.

It might feel nice for a moment to imagine someone like this getting a degree of comeuppance, but it’s a fleeting, sickly high. Barring an unforeseen development, Omar is not going to be imprisoned or deported — the big “win” will be a dramatic raid that leads to nothing. We’ve seen this enough in the second Trump administration to call it what it is: wielding the power of the executive branch to target political opponents. Any personal qualms I have with Omar pale in comparison to this abuse of power. 

Take the survey: What do you think of the claims against Rep. Omar? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The planned execution of the Fort Hood shooter.
item.dc:creator: Audrey Moorehead
item.description: A proposal divides the Trump administration.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The Fort Hood shooter’s execution. On Thursday, the Defense Department announced that it intends to livestream the execution of the former Army major who carried out the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting. The convicted shooter is scheduled to be executed by an Army firing squad on December 3, which would be the first U.S. military execution since 1961 and the first known U.S. military execution by firing squad since 1945. Republican and Democratic lawmakers have pushed back on the plan to livestream the event, and President Donald Trump said he is still considering the proposal. 

Back up: On November 5, 2009, an Army major and psychiatrist opened fire at Fort Hood in Texas, killing 13 people and injuring 32 others. The shooter was paralyzed from the waist down by return fire. He said that he carried out the attack because the U.S. military is at war with Islam, calling the United States “a government that openly acknowledges that it would hate for the law of Almighty Allah to be the supreme law of the land.” He was convicted on all charges in 2013 and sentenced to death.

Note: Due to the well documented contagion effect, Tangle does not name shooters or suspects in high-profile attacks. 

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth backed the plan to livestream the execution, saying, “We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public — because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things.” Federal regulations prohibit recording executions of inmates in the federal prison system, but the military has not explicitly barred the practice. 

On Friday, Vice President JD Vance suggested the livestream plan may not go ahead, adding that he will not watch it if it does. Separately, President Trump initially told reporters that he had approved the plan but later said he was still deciding, saying, “There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show it. ’Cause you know, by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did.”

Some Republicans have criticized the plan, including Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK), who said, “It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks.” Sen. John Curtis (R-UT) posted on X, “The victims deserve justice administered with solemnity. Broadcasting a death diminishes us and is not an effective deterrent.” Many Democrats also spoke out against the proposal, with Sen. Jack Reed (D-RI) calling it a “barbaric spectacle.” 

Today, we’ll share views from the left and right on the planned public execution, followed by Editor Audrey Moorehead’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left opposes the proposed public execution, with some saying it would be psychologically harmful to the public.
  • Many suggest the livestream would be a moral affront.
  • Others worry that the Supreme Court’s current jurisprudence would allow the firing squad execution.

In The Atlantic, Graeme Wood wrote about “the real harm of a public execution.”

“[This man] deserves what he is probably going to get in December. The rest of us, however, will be ill-served by the spectacle of his execution… Watching people die by violence, even if those people have it coming, damages the spectator irreversibly. I don’t mean physical or emotional damage,” Wood said. “I mean something more like the loss of their humanity and dignity, through partaking in the process of treating a person… like a machine to be turned off.”

“It is hard to appreciate how awful this viewing experience will be, until you have it. And then of course it will be too late. I have seen videotaped executions and have been diminished by every single one,” Wood wrote. “In this world, denying [the shooter] the pleasure of death on his own terms, and letting him instead spend a few more earthly decades in tedious incarceration, would seem a much more onerous punishment.”

In The Hill, Joslin Joseph argued that livestreaming the execution would be “replacing our own moral compass.”

“I have no problem with this man being executed and fully support calling him a terrorist. What he did was abhorrent and his justification of using his religion as an excuse doesn’t hold water to many, Muslim or otherwise,” Joseph wrote. “But livestreaming an execution is yet another way we have caved in and given up our values because of our fears… We have ‘othered’ Muslims so badly and vilified them to the point that we are now acting the way we accuse them of acting.” 

“We abhor terror groups like the Islamic State organization when they release high production snuff films showing prisoners beheaded, shot, run over by tanks, blown up with grenades, or butchered like livestock… We criticize the Saudis for public executions and call them barbaric,” Joseph said. “People flee autocratic Muslim countries because of public executions and come here because we don’t (yet) act that way.”

In his Substack, Steve Vladeck suggested that legal challenges to the execution would face “a significant obstacle.” 

“In a world in which the legality of such a public spectacle ends up in court (and I’m skeptical that it will), Hegseth’s proposal is an unusually accessible illustration of the very real consequences of the shift in the Supreme Court’s Eighth Amendment jurisprudence since 2019,” Vladeck wrote. “Ever since Justice Kennedy retired, the Court has embraced a more static, 1791-oriented conception of which punishments are — and aren’t — constitutional. 

“For decades, the Court recognized that, because the language of the Cruel and Unusual Punishments Clause is dynamic, the Clause ‘must draw its meaning from the evolving standards of decency that mark the progress of a maturing society,’” Vladeck said. “The biggest gap between the Court’s ‘evolving standards’ jurisprudence and its current approach involves punishments that were in broad use at the Founding but have since been largely repudiated. And the public execution of [the shooter] would fall right into that space.”

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with some saying executions should be public. 
  • Others worry that public execution would make a martyr out of the shooter. 
  • Still others argue that firing squads are the preferable manner of execution.

In the Daily Wire, Andrew T. Walker argued “execution demands a public witness.”

“Public outcry that reduces public execution to a ‘spectacle’ vastly undervalues the magnitude of [the shooter’s] offense. It is true that concerns about the macabre, bloodlust, and prurience are real… No one should derive joy or entertainment from watching another human die, even if the conditions are just,” Walker wrote. “Our society is no more morally enlightened than biblical times, where execution was public… and done so that ‘all Israel shall hear and fear and never again do any such wickedness as this among you’ (Deut. 13:11) — in other words, deterrence.”

“I believe capital punishment should be public,” Walker said. “The military serves the nation’s defense, not a single state, and thus citizens across the country have a right — not an obligation — to view the execution if they choose. [The shooter’s] terrorism was a symbolic act against the citizens of the United States.”

The New York Post editorial board said “don’t make… [the] execution a public spectacle.”

“America is supposed to be a model nation, with the highest values, a shining light that leads the world into a civilized future. The spectacle of a publicized, glamorized execution sends us in the opposite direction,” the board wrote. “[The] death is meant to achieve justice for the horrific evil he perpetrated, not serve as a source of entertainment or pleasure for masses… That’s not what America represents. 

“Nor will a public execution deter terror; it’ll only make a martyr out of [the shooter]. It’s precisely what monsters like [him] long for: martyrdom that brings them fame and glory. Jihadis will surely use footage of the execution as a recruiting tool. Rather than tame terrorism, it’ll only inflame it,” the board said. “For the sake of upholding America’s moral stature — and decency itself — Trump must put an end to this abominable idea.”

In the Wall Street Journal, Alex Kozinski made “the case for firing squads.”

“Perhaps states thought lethal injection would fare better in court because it resembled a familiar medical procedure. Perhaps they wanted executions to look less medieval,” Kozinski wrote. “Either way, the appeal was obvious: Put the prisoner on a gurney, attach tubes, administer drugs, and invite the public to imagine that death arrives cleanly and quickly, without anyone getting blood on his hands. Appearances, however, aren’t reality.” 

“Execution by lethal injection is dishonest. It dresses an execution in the reassuring garb of medicine, encouraging us to mistake a state killing for a clinical event. Medicine seeks to preserve life; execution ends it. This blurring of what are diametrically opposite functions is epistemologically perilous and morally repugnant,” Kozinski said. “I have some doubts whether livestreaming the execution is advisable, but Mr. Hegseth should be commended for his honesty.”

My take.
Audrey Moorehead
Editor
 
 
  • I aspire to a consistent pro-life ethic, but I still grapple with the death penalty. 
  • The Fort Hood shooter committed heinous crimes and has shown no remorse; executing him is a valid form of justice.
  • However, livestreaming the event would turn that act of justice into a spectacle.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

If you asked me to name the most important political value I hold, my answer would be simple: I am pro-life, in nearly every meaning of the term.

It seems clear to me that the single most important goal of society should be the preservation and perpetuation of human life. Life is precious, from the moment it begins until the moment it ends; to end a life prematurely is the single gravest thing that a person can do. To kill another person is to rob them of the most precious gift they have ever been given, to freeze them in place permanently, to remove their chances of experiencing further joy or bringing further joy into the world. The first murder is one of the first stories in the Bible for a reason.

In short, if you are going to kill someone, you need to have an unimpeachable reason to do so.

Given all this, I grapple with capital punishment more than any other political issue. Christian views on the death penalty are diverse and complicated, as our coverage of the failed execution of Christa Pike showcased. The Catholic Church — the largest Christian body in the world — officially opposes it. Pope Leo XIV distilled the church’s opinion on it in a social media post last weekend, writing, “The death penalty is inadmissible because it is an attack on the inviolability and dignity of the person. The common good can be safeguarded and the requirements of justice can be met without recourse to capital punishment: effective systems of detention have been developed that protect citizens while at the same time do not completely deprive those who are guilty of the possibility of redemption.”

I’m not a Catholic, but I still recognize the Pope’s formidable role in interpreting Christian moral teachings. And his emphasis that redemption is possible for any person, myself included, hits home for me.

Even so, I can’t shake the feeling that the death penalty is permissible for the most serious of crimes, and that the potential abandonment of capital punishment — indeed, our abandonment of older understandings of justice — could be detrimental to us. Amid a debate over capital punishment just after World War II, C.S. Lewis argued that to abandon the retributive theory of punishment, to instead prioritize theories of rehabilitation and deterrence, is to dehumanize the criminal and give concession to tyranny. If we pathologize all of a person’s wrongdoings, we imply that the person lacks the capacity for reason; if we solely focus on deterrence, we open ourselves to justifying the punishment of the innocents just to “set an example.” For those reasons, Lewis argued, society can’t abandon the concept of giving a criminal his “just deserts.”

If we accept that premise, then we must ask what sort of deserts are required by different crimes. Here, Lewis argues, we should rely on the principles of justice developed over centuries of legal theory and the judgments of juries of a convict’s peers. Capital punishment has been a part of this legal system since time immemorial; our ancestors understood it to be necessary, to some extent, and they further understood it to be a just desert for certain crimes. 

Of course, just because the death penalty was once understood to be necessary does not mean that its proponents were right then, or that they are right now. After all, governments have killed and still kill people for crimes that we recognize today as unworthy of the death penalty, and I think that getting the death penalty wrong — by applying it erroneously or incompetently — is the most egregious act a government can commit. Not only that, but the state making the final decision to deprive any person of the chance of redemption genuinely makes my blood run cold. 

Nevertheless, I still find myself thinking that death is the only appropriate punishment for some crimes — mass shootings among them. 

The Fort Hood shooter killed 13 people and injured 32 more, all in the name of fighting America on behalf of radical Islam. In the years since the massacre, the shooter has expressed no remorse and has in fact continued to hold fast to the extremist ideology that drove him to murder. I believe this man must choose redemption if he is to have it, but he has spent nearly two decades refusing it and doubling down at every turn. Execution, in the end, fits the bill of just deserts. In this case, the biggest miscarriage of justice is the fact he sat on death row for well over a decade.

But my support for the death penalty — even in the case of the Fort Hood shooter — is contingent on an important factor: It must be carried out with the solemnity and sobriety that such a punishment requires. We mustn’t take pleasure in ending another person’s life. Instead, we must treat it as a terrible duty, and we must afford the convicted every dignity we can, for our own consciences if not for his comfort. 

So for that reason, when I heard the Pentagon declared that the execution (by firing squad, no less) would be livestreamed, I was filled with anger. I understand the case for public executions — part of the solemnity of execution includes our understanding of the gravity of what we’re doing, and I think that modern, medicalized executions intentionally obscure and desensitize the public to the gruesome finality of the act. But there’s a difference between displaying an execution with dignity and treating it as a show of force or a spectacle. When the enactment of justice becomes a spectacle, people begin to lose their sense of justice, giving way to cravings for revenge fueled by an incendiary mob mentality.

And in my view, offering it on livestream worsens this problem. Viewing violence through a screen evokes a certain desensitization: You’re removed from the full embodied experience, making it feel unreal, like a video game or movie. Easy access to that sort of violent imagery has been found to inspire radicalization and even terrorism — it’s the very reason that the Islamic State, the group that this shooter pledges loyalty to, publicizes its killings. And the livestreamed execution of a paraplegic Islamic terrorist would do their work for them, turning the convict into a martyr and providing evidence of America’s brutality. 

Secretary Hegseth seems either unaware of or apathetic toward these problems. Neither attitude would surprise me. The secretary likes to flaunt Scripture when he thinks it emphasizes strength and bravado, but he’s just as likely to flout its demands for dignity and grace. And that misuse of Scripture, in service of such an egregious betrayal of dignity — carried out by a civil servant in a secular government, no less — makes a mockery of the idea of justice.

My hope is that the better angels in President Trump’s and Vice President Vance’s natures prevail here, and that they shoot down Hegseth’s ill-formed idea. Because if they don’t, in my view, it would be better to have no death penalty at all than to have it so abused.

Staff concurrence.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
Audrey and I disagree about the utility of the death penalty (I’ve written in stark opposition to it, including as recently as last week). But I was relieved to see we landed in the same place on the value of a public execution. While I’m almost compelled by the argument that we should have public executions to make the country reckon with what we’re allowing behind closed doors, I’m conscious of the fact that, as Audrey argued, violence begets violence (to say nothing of the fact that this particular killer wants to die a martyr). And turning it into a nationwide watch party feels like I’m stuck in an episode of Black Mirror.
 
In a surfeit of hypocrisy and violence, this is the same administration that has an HHS campaign bringing together researchers, tech companies, and advocates for a symposium on screen-related harms. Now, it’s guaranteeing a government-sponsored killing goes viral on the internet, inevitably making its way to devices across the world. If it weren’t so nauseating to imagine teenagers firing up the livestream from their phones and computers across the country, it’d be comically absurd to consider. Which, honestly, is a good way to describe Pete Hegseth’s entire term as Defense secretary.
 

Take the survey: Should the public be able to view executions? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.
